abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for compute-in-memory (CIM) architectures that fundamentally reconceptualizes data movement in processor design. Traditional computing paradigms suffer from the memory wall problem, where data transfer between memory and processing units consumes the majority of energy and latency. We propose the In-Memory Computing Paradigm (IMCP), a mathematical model that characterizes the computational capabilities of memory arrays when operated in mixed signal domains. Our theoretical analysis establishes the fundamental limits of CIM operations through information-theoretic bounds, demonstrating that certain classes of matrix-vector computations can achieve O(1) energy complexity when fully localized within memory subarrays. We derive novel complexity classes that capture the trade-offs between precision, parallelism, and energy consumption in emerging resistive memory technologies. The framework provides rigorous proofs showing that for sparse workloads, CIM architectures can achieve asymptotic improvements over state-of-the-art GPU implementations. We introduce the concept of analog-digital equivalence classes that enable formal verification of CIM correctness. This paradigm shift establishes a new theoretical foundation for computer architecture research, opening directions for architecture-aware algorithm design and compiler optimizations targeting non-von Neumann execution models.

We present a significantly improved theoretical analysis of deadline-driven scheduling in heterogeneous real-time systems, addressing critical limitations in existing scheduling theory. Prior approaches to harmonic task scheduling on heterogeneous processors fail to capture the non-trivial interaction between voltage-frequency scaling and task migration overhead. This work develops a unified analytical framework that integrates processor heterogeneity, energy consumption models, and real-time constraints into a coherent scheduling theory. We prove novel schedulability conditions for the Generalized Multiprocessor Earliest Deadline First (G-EDF) algorithm on heterogeneous platforms, achieving utilization bounds that are 23% higher than existing results. Our analysis introduces state-dependent task execution models that more accurately represent modern embedded systems with dynamic voltage and frequency selection capabilities. We derive polynomial-time feasibility tests with significantly reduced computational complexity, enabling practical application to large-scale systems. The theoretical improvements are validated through extensive simulation studies across diverse workload characteristics. This work resolves several long-standing open problems in real-time scheduling theory and provides designers with more accurate tools for system-level analysis and optimization.

This paper presents MorphicCore, a revolutionary processor architecture that fundamentally transforms how general-purpose processors adapt to diverse workload characteristics. Unlike conventional out-of-order cores with fixed pipeline depth and execution resources, MorphicCore dynamically reconfigures its microarchitecture at runtime to match application requirements. The proposed design introduces a modular execution pipeline with programmable functional unit clusters, adaptive branch predictor structures, and reconfigurable memory hierarchy organizations. We implement a prototype on a 28nm FPGA platform demonstrating live microarchitecture morphing between single-threaded aggressive execution, simultaneous multi-threading, and coarse-grained parallelism modes without halting program execution. The control plane employs lightweight machine learning predictors to anticipate workload phase transitions, enabling proactive reconfiguration with less than 2-cycle overhead. Our evaluation across SPEC CPU2017, PARSEC, and embedded benchmarks demonstrates that MorphicCore achieves an average 47% performance improvement over conventional fixed-architecture processors while maintaining equivalent power envelopes. This work establishes a new paradigm in processor design where hardware adapts to software rather than requiring software to accommodate hardware limitations, fundamentally changing the relationship between computer architecture and software optimization.

We present HydraRouter, a significantly enhanced Network-on-Chip (NoC) router architecture that substantially improves upon existing designs for manycore processor systems. While conventional adaptive routers attempt to avoid congestion, they suffer from routing complexity and deadlock avoidance overhead that limit their practical effectiveness. HydraRouter introduces a lightweight prediction mechanism that anticipates transient congestion patterns by monitoring local and neighborhood traffic statistics, enabling proactive routing decisions. The architecture employs a novel two-level virtual channel allocation strategy that prioritizes latency-sensitive traffic while ensuring fair access for best-effort communications. We design a streamlined router microarchitecture with 35% fewer pipeline stages than state-of-the-art adaptive routers, achieving competitive throughput with significantly reduced latency. Implementation results in 14nm FinFET technology demonstrate that HydraRouter achieves 2.3x improvement in packet latency under synthetic traffic patterns and 18% throughput improvement for PARSEC benchmarks compared to existing adaptive routers, while consuming only 12% additional area overhead. The proposed design maintains deadlock-freedom through a minimal credit-return mechanism that requires no routing table storage. This work provides a practical solution for high-performance manycore interconnection networks with demonstrated benefits for chip multiprocessor performance.
